extracted.intended_audience: student reporters / high-school and beginning newspaper journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing the body of a newspaper story: developing the lead, maintaining interest, ensuring accuracy and legal safety, and applying clear, coherent, economical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the body
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the story gives a detailed account of the occurrences touched upon in the lead; its relation to the lead is that of the developing sentences of a paragraph to the topic statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If notes are organized properly and the lead is forceful, writing the body is simple development in time, descriptive, expository, or suspense order. The body must develop the lead without introducing unrelated matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain interest after the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter must use every means at his command to make the body as bright and attractive as the opening sentences; do not simply add particulars as catalogue items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short paragraphs, sprightly sentences of varied length and construction, occasional direct quotations; omit obvious facts, tiresome descriptions, and unnecessary explanations; play up action; maintain any tone established by the lead (humor, pathos, tragedy). Every paragraph should begin with a strong, attractive sentence; every sentence should begin with a distinctive word or phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inaccuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: All details must be checked and rechecked for accuracy before they are written; falsehood has no place in a newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A touch of imagination in description may be harmless, but exaggeration or distortion to make events interesting is unacceptable. If a series of events cannot be made interesting without distortion of facts, it is not news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel — legal responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper is absolutely responsible for every word that appears in its columns; published matter that brings disgrace or subjects a person to public distrust, ridicule, or contempt is libel, and the paper and its staff can be held liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only full defenses are truth or accurate report of privileged matter (public meetings, judicial/legislative/executive bodies, or public gatherings). Expressions like 'it is alleged' or 'it is reported' do not mitigate libel. A libelous statement published through error and immediately retracted is still libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel — qualification and attribution of allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: When including a derogatory statement about a person the reporter should be sure of its truth; either quote the informant or clearly qualify the charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotations for the source or qualifying phrases such as 'it is alleged that' to avoid presenting unverified accusations as fact. Remember private persons accused of misdemeanors are legally presumed innocent; the paper is presumed guilty until it proves innocence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial defenses against libel (recognize limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are seven so-called partial defenses that may lessen damages but do not remove libel: (1) mistaken identity with a guilty person of same name, (2) the person's reputation was so good the statement did no harm, (3) the person was so notorious the statement could not damage him, (4) the statement was read to the person before publication and not denied, (5) the statement was provoked by the person injured, (6) the statement was made in the heat of a political campaign, (7) the statement was a mistake and retracted immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are not absolutes; every newspaper worker must know the law of libel and avoid relying on these as safe shields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid editorializing
rubrics_metrics.description: A news story that praises or blames a person, takes sides in a controversy, or attempts to influence public opinion is editorialized and should be avoided in news columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorials belong in editorial columns. Signed reviews and certain columns may contain some comment, but it should be impersonal and fair. Reporters should describe objectively, keep personal opinions out, and permit readers to draw their own inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration / conservative tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Superlatives should be used sparingly; it is far better to understate than to exaggerate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habitual use of extravagant words cheapens them; understatement lends authority. Reporters should resist enthusiasm that leads to overstatement; exaggeration makes a story ridiculous and damages the paper's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid free advertising / propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Press agents and publicity seekers often try to use news columns for free advertising or propaganda; the reporter must be suspicious and avoid printing disguised promotional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offered unsolicited stories consult the city editor before writing them. Refer commercial publicity to the business manager. Be cautious of merchant move notices, proposed improvements, or 'home-town' success stories that may be press-agent copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity of thought produces clear sentences. Newspaper sentences should be short, simple, terse, direct, and emphatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think sentences through to ensure they express exactly what is intended. Use orderly arrangement, proper sequence of tenses, paragraph grouping, and correct pronoun use. Put important statements in independent clauses and avoid vague literary phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Coherence in a news story is aided by (1) orderly arrangement of parts, (2) correct reference of pronouns, (3) repetition of key words and phrases, and (4) relation words/phrases/clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orderly arrangement is most useful. Ensure relative pronouns have unmistakable antecedents. Repetition of key words helps keep the reader's attention on the topic. Relation words are used less in news but can help when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events lacking connection should not be recorded in one story; every separate story should be kept distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not run together unrelated occurrences just because they involve the same person or place. The transition from lead to body should be smooth; the body should develop the lead as secondary sentences develop a paragraph's topic sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid choppy writing (vary sentence length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive short sentences of the same length create a monotonous 'bing-bing-bing' choppy style which should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While short sentences are desirable, vary sentence lengths and structures to avoid monotony; avoid the overuse of long periodic sentences as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a story to present facts, not to fill space; use only as many words as the importance of the event warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pad copy to fill space. The legitimate way to lengthen a story is to gather additional details. For every story ask: Is it accurate? Is it interesting? Is it clear? Is it properly condensed?

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph and sentence leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paragraph should begin with a strong, attractive sentence (a paragraph lead); likewise sentences should present their thought promptly rather than withholding it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor short statements that present thought without delay; avoid long periodic sentences that withhold the 'thunder' until the end. Make each opening word or phrase distinctive to catch the reader's attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking, attribution, and quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter must check and recheck details; when making potentially damaging or debatable statements, provide attribution or direct quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote informants for derogatory statements or qualify them as allegations; do not publish unverified accusations as fact. Treat signed statements and paid advertisements carefully—paper is liable even for those.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and correct usage (specific rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correct words and idioms; a list of common misuses and correct forms is provided to maintain precision and professionalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Examples from the text:
- 'Comprise' means include or comprehend (The organization comprises five departments); use 'compose' or 'make up' for 'Five students compose the committee.'
- 'Due to' modifies a noun — do not use where 'because of' or 'on account of' is required.
- Avoid 'cute' as weak slang; prefer more precise adjectives (pretty, vivacious).
- 'Either'/'neither' properly refer to two items only; use 'none' for three or more.
- 'Enthuse' is considered vulgarism; prefer 'arouse enthusiasm.'
- Use 'etc.' sparingly; prefer definite terms.
- Do not use 'get' with an infinitive ('I did not get to go' → 'I did not get a chance to go').
- 'Help' (meaning avoid) should be followed by a gerund, not 'but' ('We cannot help losing').
- 'If' is not a synonym for 'whether'.
- Distinguish 'indulge in' (put no restraint upon oneself) vs 'practice/engage in' (e.g., 'engage in gardening').
